summary: Most travelers must arrange a visa before arriving in the Republic of the Congo, either through a Congolese embassy or the recently introduced electronic visa channel, while fellow CEMAC citizens from Cameroon, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea, Chad and the Central African Republic enter freely.

notes: Exporting ivory, wildlife products and some hardwoods is prohibited without permits.
Large amounts of CFA franc cash fall under BEAC currency-control rules — declare significant sums on arrival and departure.

payments.text: Outside a handful of international hotels in Brazzaville and Pointe-Noire, cards are of little use — the Republic of the Congo runs on cash, so carry CFA francs and some euros to exchange.

safety.text: Brazzaville and Pointe-Noire are reasonably calm but petty crime occurs, and parts of the Pool region have seen unrest in the past — check current advisories, avoid travel after dark outside cities and carry ID at all times.

bestTimeToVisit.text: The June-to-September dry season is the most comfortable time, with easier road travel and the best conditions for Odzala-Kokoua and the northern forests.

idp.text: Republic of the Congo is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1968 Vienna one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1949 Geneva version. A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here.

driving.text: Republic of the Congo is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1968 Vienna one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1949 Geneva version. A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Republic of the Congo yet.

tips.text: Do not confuse the Republic of the Congo (Brazzaville) with the Democratic Republic of the Congo (Kinshasa) across the river — they are separate countries with separate visas, and the ferry crossing between the two capitals requires valid documents for both.
The yellow fever certificate is checked on arrival — travelers without a valid yellow card can be refused entry.
Police checkpoints are common — carry your passport (or a certified copy) with the visa and entry stamp at all times, as documents are frequently inspected.
Bring euros in cash to exchange and withdraw CFA francs in Brazzaville or Pointe-Noire before heading anywhere else — ATMs are unreliable and cards are rarely accepted.
Photographing government buildings, bridges, airports, the port and anything military is prohibited and can lead to detention — ask before photographing people.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for the Republic of the Congo?
faq.answer: Almost certainly yes. Apart from CEMAC citizens (Cameroon, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea, Chad and the Central African Republic), who enter freely, travelers must obtain a visa in advance from a Congolese embassy — an electronic visa channel has been introduced but its roll-out is uneven, so confirm the current procedure before booking.

faq.question: Can I get a visa on arrival in Congo-Brazzaville?
faq.answer: No — there is no reliable visa on arrival for tourists. Arrange your visa through a Congolese embassy before traveling; airlines will normally refuse boarding without one.

faq.question: Is this the same country as the DRC?
faq.answer: No. The Republic of the Congo (capital Brazzaville) and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (capital Kinshasa) are different countries facing each other across the Congo River, each with its own visa. A visa for one is not valid for the other.

faq.question: Is yellow fever vaccination required for the Republic of the Congo?
faq.answer: Yes — a yellow fever certificate is required from all travelers aged 9 months and over and is checked on arrival. Keep the yellow card with your passport.

faq.question: Is the Republic of the Congo safe to visit?
faq.answer: Brazzaville, Pointe-Noire and the northern national parks are generally calm, but petty crime occurs and parts of the Pool region have a history of unrest. Check your government’s current travel advisory, avoid night road travel and keep identity documents on you.
